title: Why Arribes tastes the way it does

lede.text: Vines here grow in a granite canyon that is about 5 °C warmer than the plateau above it. That heat gives the reds ripe, stewed-fruit aromas, and the westerly rain keeps the acidity fresh.

chapters.title: A canyon cut into the plateau
paras: The land drops from about 700 m on the plateau to only 130 m at the riverbanks within a few kilometres. The Duero and the Tormes cut this canyon into a granite base, along with smaller rivers such as the Uces and the Huebra. These slopes are the arribes. It is not a mountain zone, but the drops are steep and the hillsides are many.
The plateau is called the penillanura. The canyon walls and the plateau give the vines two different climates.

fly.label: The Arribes canyon
fly.caption: The Duero and its tributaries cut a canyon into the granite, from about 700 m down to 130 m.

chapters.title: The warmest corner of Castilla y León
paras: This is the westernmost end of the Duero basin, so rain is relatively high: 575 to 800 mm a year. The climate is sub-humid Mediterranean, warmer and wetter than the rest of the region. Average temperatures are the highest in all of Castilla y León, because the land is low, the Atlantic reaches in and the valleys make their own microclimate.

On the plateau the winters are long and cold and the summers short and hot. In the canyons it is about 5 °C warmer, the winters are shorter and the summers longer. The canyons know no frost. January averages about 9 °C and August about 26 °C, with about 2,680 hours of sun a year. The valley walls also shelter the vines from cold winds.

The spring comes early and the rain arrives in time, so the natural acidity does not usually fall below 5.5 g/l. The warmth ripens the grapes fully and concentrates the polyphenols. Wines lean towards overripe, stewed fruit.

chapters.title: Thin, stony granite
paras: The base rock is granite, with some slate. The soils are silty sand and very stony. The vines root in only about 30 cm of soil, a little more over slate.

The soil is pale yellow-brown, acid (pH 5 to 6) and poor in lime. It holds little organic matter, 1.5 to 3%. Juan García, the main red grape, thrives even on the poorest ground and gives steady yields. It gives the wines structure and softness.

fly.label: Fermoselle
fly.caption: Fermoselle is one of the towns where the vineyards recovered fully after phylloxera, by about 1913-14.

chapters.title: Old bush vines and the barrel
paras: At least half of the vineyard was planted before 1956. Almost all of it is bush-trained, with 2,000 to 3,000 plants per hectare. Trellised vines are rare.
Phylloxera came from Portugal and entered the region through the Arribes in 1888. The vineyards recovered by about 1913-14 and ended up mostly red.
A white labelled Fermentado en Barrica is both fermented and aged on its lees in oak barrels of 600 l at most, for at least three months. It shows smoky, toasty notes with fruit and well-blended oak.
The whites are fruity or floral, sometimes with a mineral note. The reds are rich in polyphenols with ripe fruit aromas.

terms.text: A rosé or red that has spent at least three months in oak barrels.
